title: Unveiling the foveal rod scotoma through flicker
abstract: Under low-light conditions, vision relies on rod receptors only. The foveal region in the center of the visual field, however, is devoid of rods. Nevertheless, humans usually do not perceive any gap in their center of vision at night, because the missing information is filled-in from the surround. In the present study, we show that the rod scotoma can be rendered perceivable with a continuous flicker. The flicker interferes with the filling-in process, leaving a grayish spot at the rod scotoma's location in the subsequent phase. The spot appears blurry, phantom-like, and circular. After we had determined suitable frequencies for each participant, they reproduced the spot sizes with peripherally viewed disks. Participants more often reported seeing the spot when the flicker frequency was similar to their preferred frequency. Neither the levels of dark adaptation, as tested with rod stimuli in a mesopic condition, nor the macular pigmentation accumulating in the fovea influenced the reported spot sizes. On average, the spots were 2.5 dva in diameter. This is substantially larger than the average anatomical scotoma of 1.25 dva, likely reflecting the rod-sparse regions around the fovea. We demonstrate that flicker is sufficient to make the rod scotoma visible, similar to the S-cone scotoma. The findings emphasize that percepts in central rod vision may not represent veridical information across areas larger than the anatomical rod-free region.
